title: each as a lens for a week
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: a story people tell about a scholar who wrote careful books on schools that disagreed, and named one of them after his wife
carry: each as a lens for a week

segments.voice: Yesterday, each as a lens for a week brought the last pair: Mimamsa asks what this act is for, Vedanta asks what it rests on, and a Gita verse holds both.

There's a story people tell about a scholar named Vachaspati Mishra. He was writing a commentary, and he worked at it so long and so completely that he lost track of everything else, including the woman who kept the lamp lit beside him, his wife. When he finally looked up and asked who she was, she told him. Moved, so the story goes, he named the book after her: the Bhamati. The story may be legend. But the scholar's shelf is real, and it's strange. On the last day of this part, it shows how to hold all six darshanas at once.
screen: `A SCHOLAR BENT OVER HIS BOOK.` → `THE ONE WHO KEPT THE LAMP LIT.` → `A BOOK NAMED FOR HER.`

segments.voice: Here's what's strange about the shelf. The Bhamati is a Vedanta commentary, in Shankara's line. But Vachaspati Mishra is also remembered for commentaries on Nyaya, on Samkhya, on Yoga and on Mimamsa. Schools that argue with each other, sometimes sharply. And he wrote on each of them from the inside, carefully, laying out its case in its own terms. That's what a lens is. Not a team jersey. A way of seeing you learn well enough to look through. So here are all six, one last time. Nyaya: how do I know? Vaisheshika: what is this made of? Samkhya: who is watching? Yoga: what is the mind doing? Mimamsa: what is this act for? Vedanta: what does all of it rest on? Each one, these weeks, brought something into focus that the others left soft. And now the title's invitation, plainly. Each as a lens for a week: a school a day, its question carried from morning until night, and a last day with no lens at all. It ends with no winner. That's the point of the part we're closing, schools of thought, never ranked. The tradition kept all six on one shelf, argued among them for a long time, and kept the lamp lit for the next reader. Tomorrow the lineage track picks up again, with a different teacher, Krishna speaking to his friend Uddhava in the Bhagavata, on action.
screen: `ONE SCHOLAR, MANY SCHOOLS.` · `A LENS, NOT A TEAM JERSEY.` · `ALL SIX QUESTIONS.` · `A DAY FOR EACH LENS.`

segments.voice: Picture the first ordinary thing you'll do tomorrow morning, filling a kettle, finding your keys, opening a door, and let whichever of the six questions arrives first stand in front of it. Look through it for a few breaths and notice what comes into focus, then set the lens down and rest in the plain scene without any question at all. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight.
Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta, each tried for a day, none of them ranked. Today's word.
screen: `EACH AS A LENS FOR A WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: each as a lens for a week. A lens, not a team jersey. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1201 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA: THE BHAGAVATA'S UDDHAVA GITA.`

howItsDone: Traditional students of Indian philosophy learn the darshanas from their own root texts and commentaries, and classical scholars such as Vachaspati Mishra wrote commentaries on several schools, setting out each one's case in its own terms.

what a scholar hears: Vachaspati Mishra's commentaries across the darshanas, including the Bhamati on Shankara's Brahma Sutra Bhashya, the Tattva-kaumudi on Samkhya and the Tattva-vaisharadi on Yoga.

notes: The Bhamati naming story is traditional legend; the script says so twice. Confirm the telling (details vary).

Vachaspati Mishra's commentaries: Bhamati (Advaita), Tattva-kaumudi (Samkhya), Tattva-vaisharadi (Yoga), Nyaya-vartika-tatparya-tika (Nyaya), Nyaya-kanika and Tattva-bindu (Mimamsa). No Vaisheshika commentary is claimed. Confirm.
